newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine awaits Yeltsin, ready to make friends.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine awaits Yeltsin, ready to make friends.

text.p: Ukraine plays host on Friday to Russian President Boris Yeltsin who is due to sign a treaty of friendship after years of bickering over the Soviet Black Sea Fleet.

Yeltsin has cancelled six visits to sign the treaty since Kiev became independent of Moscow in 1991, but the prime ministers of the two countries paved the way for his arrival by signing a series of key accords on Wednesday.

The Russian leader held five summits with President Leonid Kuchma and his predecessor Leonid Kravchuk on Russian and Ukrainian territory aimed at solving the fleet issue but none of those deals dealt with the problem in the long term.

Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko and his Russian counterpart, Viktor Chernomyrdin, made a breakthrough by agreeing Moscow could keep its lion's share of the now rusting Soviet-era navy at the Crimean port of Sevastopol for the next 20 years.

Yeltsin, fresh from concluding a major treaty with NATO, said on Thursday the government talks had paved the way for a "breakthrough" during his visit. He arrives in Kiev on Friday evening and is due to sign the treaty on Saturday morning.
The decision stirred emotions among nationalists in Kiev who according to the respected Den daily were planning to greet Yeltsin "like hooligans" with protests against his visit.
"Russia has taken Sevastopol" read its Friday headline -- the words "on a 20-year lease" added in smaller letters below.
Confusion reigned over exactly what the two premiers had agreed about the fleet and where the two navies should be based.
Chernomyrdin told reporters that one bay would be shared by the two navies -- but Lazarenko later said he was mistaken.
Ukrainian First Deputy Defence Minister Ivan Bizhan told a briefing on Thursday that Russia's share would be based in Sevastopolskaya, Yuzhnaya and Karantinnaya bays.

Ukraine's share would be moored at Streletskaya bay nearby and at Balaclava base outside the city. He also said the deal could be extended by five years if both sides were willing to accept such a deal a year before the lease expired.
The settlement was generally welcomed in Sevastopol itself.
"By signing a lease agreement Russia has recognised the Ukrainian status of Sevastopol," Nikolai Savchenko, head of the Ukrainian navy's press service at the port, said by telephone.

Russian nationalists have repeatedly staked their claim to Sevastopol, saying it was excluded from a document in which Ukrainian-raised Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev ceded the Crimean peninsula as a "gift" to Ukraine in 1954.
Savchenko added: "Dragging out the issue of the transfer of the ships has left the vessels in a terrible state and it will cost a lot to restore them".

Kravchuk and Yeltsin agreed in June 1993 that the fleet would be split 50-50 but two years later a new deal was struck with Kuchma under which Ukraine got 18.3 percent in return for a reduction in its energy debt to Moscow.
Ukrainian sailors suspect their Russian colleagues of deliberately not taking good care of the 52 ships set aside for the delayed second stage of the transfer.
Admiral Viktor Kravchenko, commander of the Russian fleet, said he planned to lower the Soviet flag from his ships and replace it with the Russian imperial fleet's symbol on June 12.
"I think the historical St Andrew's flag should be raised on the Black Sea Fleet's ships on Russian Independence Day," his press service quoted him as saying.

That event was likely to be greeted with dismay by Ukrainian patriots in the majority Russian city. "The presence of foreign servicemen is of course not the most auspicious scenario for a state's independence," Savchenko said.
